blocks.text: GUGGENHEIM 2026: Jennifer West

© Jennifer West, (Installation view) Solo exhibition: Stitched Cosmos , 2026, Ca’ Foscari University, Venice, Italy, Curated by Francesco Urbano Ragazzi. Photo: Gaia Cambiaggi. Courtesy of the artist.

In recent months, we have been featuring the work of many of the 2026 Guggenheim Fellows as a way to celebrate their achievements and understand legacies and projects that have brought them this tremendous recognition.

The Board of Trustees of the John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation announced their appointment of the 101st class of Guggenheim Fellows, including 223 distinguished individuals working across 55 disciplines. Chosen through a rigorous application and peer review process from a pool of nearly 5,000 applicants, the Class of 2026 Guggenheim Fellows was tapped based on both prior career achievement and exceptional promise. As established in 1925 by founder Senator Simon Guggenheim, each Fellow receives a monetary stipend to pursue independent work at the highest level under “the freest possible conditions.”

“Our new class of Guggenheim Fellows is representative of the world’s best thinkers, innovators, and creators in art, science, and scholarship,” said Edward Hirsch, award-winning poet and President of the Guggenheim Foundation. “As the Foundation enters its second century and looks to the future, I feel confident that this new class of 223 individuals will do bold and inspiring work, undaunted by the challenges ahead. We are honored to support their visionary contributions.”

Q: What did receiving a Guggenheim Fellowship mean to you at this stage in your artistic career?

JW: I’m currently making a large two-part project that the Guggenheim Fellowship has provided the resources to fully realize. When I got the news, I was just two months away from opening the exhibition of the project’s first phase, Stitched Cosmos —which had formed the basis of my fellowship application. It was incredible in all ways to start the fellowship with the installation and opening of the exhibition, at Ca’Foscari University, coinciding with the 61 st Venice Biennale—curated by the duo, Francesco Urbano Ragazzi . I couldn’t have asked for better timing. Receiving this fellowship is an incredible honor, and one that I do not take lightly.

Q: Did receiving the Guggenheim Fellowship validate something you already knew about your practice and your work?

JW: Receiving the fellowship didn’t necessarily validate something I already knew about myself, but being selected by a committee of previous recipients makes the recognition especially meaningful to me. It’s humbling to join the company of fellows, which includes “sheroes” like Maya Deren and Carolee Schneemann, mentors like Diana Thater, Mike Kelley and Mary Kelly and many fellow artists. Not to mention the many it has awarded, from so many disciplines—artists, writers and thinkers—from history to now, whom I have read, studied and admired deeply. I had applied on and off since 2009 (17 years), so I was surprised and somewhat in shock when I saw the email. I feel honored and didn’t do this alone, so acknowledging all the community that has kept me going—those whose work, shows, writing, skills have continued to affect me, and to all those that have I have worked with in big and small ways.

Q: What has sustained your practice the most over the years?

JW: Experimentation is what keeps me going. I use art as a foil to reflect on the continual changes in the world, in the materiality of images, and our cultural relationships to them. I’m always thinking how can I give analog film an afterlife in our digital world? As analog film recedes further into our cultural and technological rearview mirror, I lean into its archives, traces, communities and evolution.

© Jennifer West, Two production stills featuring 35mm filmstrips soaking in urine. From Jennifer West, Emoji Piss Film (35mm film print soaked and corroded with urine by Andrea Bowers, Symrin Chawla, Micah Espudo, Chris Hanke, Eli Joteva, Jack McGuinn, Peyton Regan, Julian Toca, Vidhi Todi, Bob Viera, Ariel West, Fleurette West, Peter West, and Jwest) 2018, 2 minutes, 33 seconds 35mm film transferred to high-definition digital video, remastered to 6K and 16mm optical print (2024)

JW: Sometimes, this took the form of archiving experiences searching digital material of the internet onto filmstrips by using screen recordings of ephemeral programs like Google searches, Maps and Earth, astronomy software, Wikipedia or film titles. Lately I’ve been working in collections and archives to make things seen, and to add images that are not already online.

© Jennifer West, (Installation view) Solo exhibition, Golden Conversion , CAPITAL Gallery, San Francisco, CA, 2018. Emoji Wall of Film , 2018, 70mm filmstrips, ink, dye, cat litter, salt, spray paint, latex paint, gel medium, staples, paper, white-out, pigment prints on clear film, dimensions variable Photo: Jonathan Runcio

© Jennifer West, (Detail) Solo exhibition, Golden Conversion , CAPITAL Gallery, San Francisco, CA, 2018. Emoji Wall of Film , 2018, 70mm filmstrips, ink, dye, cat litter, salt, spray paint, latex paint, gel medium, staples, paper, white-out, pigment prints on clear film, dimensions variable Photo: Jonathan Runcio

JW: I have been working with moving images for 23 years and am known for my physical interventions directly onto celluloid film, which I often exhibit as large-scale installations in art spaces often alongside my mixed media works and artist books. To date, I have produced 85 films with run-times ranging in length from 17 seconds to 67 minutes made with and without the use of a camera. Concurrently, I have made numerous quilts, tapestries, walls of film, and interactive installations. As part of a generation that witnessed the seismic shift from analog to digital technologies, I mine the dual properties of film: its materiality as celluloid film strips and its fleeting immateriality (when screened).

© Jennifer West, (Installation view on left) Marinated Film – the roll of 16mm I had in the fridge for over ten years (16mm film negative marinated for several months in: Absinthe & XTC, Pepsi & Poprocks, Jim Shaw’s Urine, Red Wine, Coffee & Detox Tea, Aphrodisiacs) , 2005, 9 minutes, 20 seconds 16mm transferred to video; (Detail view on right) Recipe Cards (for the Marinated Film) Pencil on index cards, each 3 x 5 inches Photos: Joshua White

© Jennifer West, Film stills from Marinated Film – the roll of 16mm I had in the fridge for over ten years (16MM film negative marinated for several months in: Pepsi & Poprocks, Jim Shaw’s Urine, Red Wine, Coffee & Detox Tea) 2005, 9 minutes, 20 seconds 16mm film transferred to digital video, Celine and Julie Go Boating, Anna Helwing Gallery, Los Angeles, CA 2005, Curated by Michael Ned Holte

JW: My approach to working directly with celluloid film using everyday materials—corroding, staining, dyeing, and marking its surface—started in 2005 as an experiment to see what would happen to several cans of unexposed 16mm film that had been sitting in my fridge for over a decade. The already aged film was processed at my film lab without exposing it to images, then I distributed sections to several people in my community, asking them to make “marinades” in which to soak the film. The resulting altered filmstrips—produced using everything from Jim Shaw’s urine to bath salts and Gatorade—were scanned to video for exhibition.

© Jennifer West, Three production stills from Marinated Film – the roll of 16mm I had in the fridge for over ten years (16MM film negative marinated for several months in: Pepsi & Poprocks, Jim Shaw’s Urine, Red Wine, Coffee & Detox Tea) 2005, 9 minutes, 20 seconds 16mm film transferred to digital video. (Left) Raspberries in blue Gatorade from Ariel West (Middle) Jim Shaw ’s urine, (Right) Paul Masson white wines from Jennifer Krasinki

JW: My early films explored cultural relationships to taste, touch and smell, eventually expanding to music, text and through public participation—public interactive films. Over time, these experiments took many forms: cooking the film with eggs, spraying it with laxatives and antacids, submerging it in the waters of the spiral jetty, oceans, rivers, soaking it in coffee and energy drinks, and even exposing it to gamma rays. I also invited people to interact directly with the film by writing on it, kissing it, skateboarding over it, or, leaving marks it in various other ways.

Q: How did the shift from analog to digital media directly impact your artistic practice?

JW: A pivotal moment for the development of my “Media archeology” work was in 2013, when the film industry at large began to shift away from celluloid film and into the digital sphere. This shift significantly reduced access to film stock, processing labs, and technicians versed in the medium, all of which I relied upon to make my work. In response, I began creating artworks that offered viewers a direct, physical experience of film as a material. I began creating immersive installations featuring large walls of filmstrips displayed alongside their scanned moving images: Film is Dead… (2017/2019/2021) and Emoji Wall of Film (2018), as well as interactive projection works like Flashlight Filmstrip Projections (2014/2016/2023). Through these earlier bodies of work, I explored how static, sculptural arrangements of celluloid images could be activated and transformed by light. My more recent work, Stitched Cosmos, builds on this foundation by merging the physical materiality of film with the conceptual framework of the traditions of quilting and the imagery of space imaging.

© Jennifer West, (Installation view) Flashlight Filmstrip Projections , 2016. 35 and 70mm filmstrips, inks, dyes, permanent marker, acrylic, inkjet prints on clear film, tape, flashlights; Tramway, Glasgow, Scotland, 2016. Photo: Keith Hunter

“Now I am like an old, seasoned witch in the Federici way, holding the knowledge, magic, imperfection and slowness of the analog, continuing to morph it into the digital and physical world.” — Jennifer West from a conversation with curators Francesco Urbano Ragazzi for King Kong ’21, 2026

Q: How do you plan to use the time granted to you from the Guggenheim Fellowship this next year?

JW: I’m currently working on the second part of my larger project . Weaving Outer Space, a research-based project, that will result in an exhibition consisting of a large-scale installation of suspended celluloid film quilts and weavings, moving-image works, and illuminated light panels. The exhibition builds upon Stitched Cosmos (2026), the first chapter of the project developed during my Smithsonian Artist Research Fellowship (2025–26). Weaving Outer Space investigates the parallels between quilting, astronomical imaging, and filmmaking—all processes that use stitching, weaving, mathematics, and patternmaking to map out space and time.

© Jennifer West, Preying Mantis, Spider, Dragon, Mistakes Light Diptych , 2026, Diptych light panel with Monomeric print (transferred from astronomical glass film negatives), aluminum. 85.237 x 22.64 in. (single image size) and dimensions variable. Solo exhibition, Stitched Cosmos Ca’Foscari University, Venice, Italy, 2026 Curated by Francesco Urbano Ragazzi Photo: Gaia Cambiaggi

JW: To be developed during my current Guggenheim Fellowship (2026–27), this second chapter expands my research through the archives of the Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum and the Space Telescope Science Institute. While Stitched Cosmos focused on the Harvard College Observatory Astronomical Plate Collection and the women who classified the stars, Weaving Outer Space shifts attention to the people, many of them women, whose labor, materials, and processes are behind the technologies that make space imaging possible.
Artist Jennifer West working in the Harvard Plate Stacks, Center for Astrophysics, Cambridge, MA during West’s Smithsonian Artist Research Fellowship. Photo: Lisa Hees

JW: Working with over 10,000 analog and digital still images I photographed of archival objects in Washington, D.C., and Baltimore, I am exploring the connections between weaving, stitching, coding, mapping, repair, painting, and astronomical image-making. Through this research, I bring together historical technologies, handmade objects, and images of outer space, in order to investigate the intersections of craft, technology, and the often-unseen labor embedded within technological progress. A newly commissioned score by composer Celia Hollander will accompany the moving-image installation.

© Jennifer West, (Installation view) Interlaced: Animation and Textiles 07 Dec 2024 – 27 Apr 2025, Govett-Brewster Art Gallery/Len Lye Centre, New Plymouth, New Zealand, Curated by Alla Gadassik (catalog). (Detail) Orange Haze Film Quilt , 2024, 35 and 70mm filmstrips, inkjet print on clear film, ink, dyes, volcanic ash hand-made dye, permanent marker, moth wing, thread, plexiglas 53 x 33 in
Q: Does your Guggenheim Fellowship project have a personal significance to you?

JW: During the reception, I was focused on meeting as many fellows as possible in all kinds of fields. I spoke with philosophers, archaeologists, biographers, engineers, environmental scientists, biologists, poets, choreographers, puppeteers, musicians, filmmakers, scholars, and, of course, visual artists and photographers. It was a pleasure to have a rapid exchange of ideas and perspectives with so many people working in different fields. On a personal level, the fellowship has given further weight to my project (proposed and ongoing chapters) and provided the resources to support its completion. It was a North Star.

One aspect of the fellowship I particularly appreciate is its open call application process, which sets it apart from the many awards and fellowships available only through nomination. I can only imagine the complexity of maintaining such a process and, I appreciate the Guggenheim Foundation’s commitment to keeping it accessible. At a time when funding for artists is increasingly under attack, I believe it is more important than ever that institutions like this are able to sustain their mission—for the incredible support of artists and intellectuals.

© Jennifer West, Stitched Cosmos Holofans 1-3 (scanned glass astronomical negatives and JWST satellite images) , 2026, 6k video (transferred from astronomical glass film negatives), HOLOFAN projector. Dimensions variable. (Installation view) Solo Exhibition, Stitched Cosmos , May 7 – July 6, 2026, Ca’ Foscari University, Venice, Italy. Curated by Francesco Urbano Ragazzi Photos: Gaia Cambiaggi
Q: Is your practice at a pivotal point? How do you see your work shifting from what you have done in the past to what you plan to work in during your Fellowship year?

JW: I’m not sure yet. In 2013, I started working more in archives, researching pre-cinema objects and their histories at the Getty Research Institute, and incorporating my findings into installations. Over the past number of years, I have worked almost entirely in collections and archives, driven by a desire to document and make visible materials and histories that are not already on the internet. My Guggenheim Fellowship project is derived directly from the research and the images I’ve gathered from archival collections. We will see if there is a pivot in the future.
© Jennifer West and Yuz Museum, In Production: Art and the Studio System , (Installation View) Yuz Museum, Shanghai, 2019-2020, Curated by Rita Gonzalez, Photo by JJYPhoto
Q: Have you applied for a Guggenheim Fellowship previously? If so, did you alter your submission in any way from a previous application?
JW: I have applied on and off since 2009. The application I submitted that was awarded the Fellowship was new, but was based on an ongoing project.
Q: Your work is/has been very based in the medium of photography. Can you explain your choice to apply under the Fine Art category versus under the photography category?
JW: I applied to both Fine Art and Film and Video categories—as an artist who works with film and presents in an art context.

Jennifer West (b. Topanga, CA, 1966) is a 2026 Guggenheim Fellow and a 2025-26 Smithsonian Artist Research Fellow. She is a Los Angeles–based artist whose work continues to challenge the distinctions between analog and digital image-making while tracing the cultural and material histories embedded within media itself. For over two decades, she has transformed 16mm, 35mm, and 70mm film into installations, sculptures, and participatory works that reimagine film as a living, communal medium.

© Jennifer West, (Installation view) Solo exhibition: Stitched Cosmos , 2026, Ca’ Foscari University, Venice, Italy, Curated by Francesco Urbano Ragazzi. Photo: Gaia Cambiaggi. Courtesy of the artist.

In 2026, West presented a solo exhibition, Stitched Cosmos concurrent with the Venice Biennial 61 at Ca’Foscari University in Venice, Italy. West’s projects have been commissioned by Tate Modern, the High Line, ICA London, Seattle Art Museum, LIAF Biennial Norway, Aspen Art Museum and Frieze Los Angeles, among others. Solo exhibitions of her work have been shown at Pompidou Paris, Yuz Museum (Shanghai), Tramway Glasgow, Man de Museo (Sardinia, Italy), Contemporary Art Museum, St Louis and Houston, Kunstverein Nurnberg (Germany), JOAN Los Angeles and White Columns, NY and included in major group exhibitions at the Barbican in London, CAPC in Bordeaux, France, Kunsthalle Schirn in Frankfurt, ZKM in Karlsruhe, the Whitney Museum and the Drawing Center in New York. Her work is held in major museum collections including LACMA, Yuz Museum (Shanghai), MOCA, Saatchi Collection London, Kadist Collection Paris/SF, Columbus Museum of Art, the Hammer, and the Getty. A monograph on her work, Media Archaeology was published by Radius Books in 2022. West received an MFA from Art Center in Pasadena where she studied with Diana Thater and Mike Kelley and a BA from the Evergreen State College in Olympia, Washington and is currently a Professor of Practice at the USC Roski School of Art and Design in Los Angeles.
